deep.reconstruction:
PART A (end of §46, Exemplum). §46 on the previous page: given a and b, find all x with ax+b a square. If one solution q is known, with aq+b=p^2, then x = a y^2 ± 2p y + q gives a(ay^2 ± 2py + q) + b = (ay ± p)^2. Example a=7, b=2: 7·1+2 = 3^2, so q=1 and p=3. Hence x = 7y^2 ± 6y + 1, and 7x+2 = (7y ± 3)^2. Table: y=0 gives 1; y=1 gives 7±6+1 = 2 or 14; y=2 gives 29±12 = 17 or 41; y=3 gives 64±18 = 46 or 82; y=4 gives 113±24 = 89 or 137. Sorted, the values are 1, 2, 14, 17, 41, 46, 82, 89, 137, ... Their differences alternate as 1, 12, 3, 24, 5, 36, 7, 48, 9, 60, ...: odd numbers 2k-1 interleaved with 12k. [Mine: the next values are 146 and 206 at y=5, giving the differences 9 and 60 Euler lists. The pairs are 7k^2-6k+1 and 7k^2+6k+1.] [Mine: completeness holds here because 7 is prime, so s^2 ≡ 2 (mod 7) has only the classes s ≡ ±3.]

PART B (§47): find two triangular numbers whose product is triangular, T_x T_y = T_z with T_n = n(n+1)/2.
- Step 1. The condition is x(x+1)y(y+1) = 2z(z+1). Multiply by pq and split the product into two factorizations: p x(y+1) = 2q z and q y(x+1) = p(z+1). Their product reproduces the equation.
- Step 2. This gives z = px(y+1)/(2q) and z = qy(x+1)/p - 1. Equating (multiply by 2pq): 2q^2 y(x+1) - 2pq = p^2 x(y+1).
- Step 3. Rewritten: xy(2q^2-p^2) + 2q^2 y - 2pq - p^2 x = 0. Put a = 2q^2 - p^2. Then a xy + 2q^2 y - p^2 x - 2pq = 0, so y = (p^2 x + 2pq)/(a x + 2q^2).
- Step 4. Hence a y - p^2 = (2apq - 2p^2 q^2)/(ax + 2q^2), that is, p^2 - a y = 2pq(pq-a)/(ax + 2q^2).
- Step 5. Factor 2pq(pq-a) = f g and set f = ax + 2q^2. Then g = p^2 - a y, so x = (f - 2q^2)/a and y = (p^2 - g)/a.
- Step 6. Euler remarks that a = 1 is easy to arrange. [Mine: this means solving p^2 - 2q^2 = -1, the negative Pell equation for 2: (1,1), (7,5), (41,29), ...] [Mine: with a = 1, p is odd and gcd(p,q) = 1. From p^2 x(y+1) = 2q(qy(x+1) - p) it follows that 2q | x(y+1), so z is automatically an integer.]

Example: p=7, q=5, a=1. Then fg = 2·35·34 = 2380 = 4·5·7·17, x = f - 50, y = 49 - g.
- g=20, f=119 gives x=69, y=29. T_69 = 35·69 and T_29 = 15·29. z = px(y+1)/(2q) = 7·69·30/10 = 7·69·3 = 1449, and T_1449 = 1449·725 = 69·35·29·15 = 1050525.
- Next page: g=28, f=85 gives x=35, y=21, z=539, and T_539 = 539·270 = 35·18·11·21.
- [Mine: other divisor pairs also work, e.g. g=34 gives (20,15,224), g=35 gives (18,14,189), g=17 gives (90,32,2079).]
errors: In the printed example the formula is written z = px(y+1)/2. It should read z = px(y+1)/(2q), i.e. divided by 10. The numerical evaluation 7·69·3 = 1449 correctly uses 7·69·30/10, so this is only a typographical slip in the formula.

Not an error on this page, but the general claim in §46 (previous page) that x = a y^2 ± 2p y + q contains 'omnes solutiones' is false for general composite a. When b has more than two square roots mod a, other residue classes are missed; e.g. a=15, b=1 gives s ≡ ±1, ±4 (mod 15). For the example a=7 (prime) the claim is correct.
Euler leaves implicit that x>0 and y>0 require f > 2q^2 and g < p^2, and that z is an integer. With a=1 the integrality of z is in fact automatic.

results.what: Parametrization of all x with 7x+2 a square: x = 7y^2 ± 6y + 1, with the interleaved difference pattern 1, 12, 3, 24, ...
results.modern_name: Solving a quadratic congruence s^2 ≡ b (mod a) and lifting a residue class
results.usually_credited_to: folklore; Euler/Lagrange/Gauss theory of quadratic residues

results.what: Method for T_x·T_y = T_z by splitting x(x+1)y(y+1) = 2z(z+1) into two bilinear relations with a parameter ratio p:q. With 2q^2 - p^2 = 1 (negative Pell), every factorization fg = 2pq(pq-1) yields a solution x = f - 2q^2, y = p^2 - g. Examples: (69,29,1449), (35,21,539).
results.modern_name: Triangular numbers whose product is triangular (Diophantine equation T_x T_y = T_z); factorization/parametric family via the Pell equation p^2 - 2q^2 = -1
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (Opera postuma, 1862); later studied by Sierpiński, Breiteig, Ulas and others

deep.surprise_reason: Both items appeared in print in the 1862 Opera postuma and belong to classical Diophantine material. The triangular-product method is a neat elementary device, likely recorded in Dickson's History among Euler's contributions, but not a result credited to anyone later.

every divisor g<49 of 2380 gives T_x T_y = T_z with integer z
